🌀 Phi Collapse — Visual

Drag to explore · Watch the fractal form at row 0

ROW 0 — COLLAPSE POINT
Identity holds Fractal edge Breaks
1What you're seeing. Each pixel tests whether a+b−c=d survives XOR at that point. Bright = yes. Dark = no. The purple fringe is the fractal boundary where it flickers.
2Row 0 is the anchor. Move the collapse depth slider — as you go deeper (rows 1–6), the bright zone shrinks and fragments. Row 0 has the largest stable region. That's the phi collapse.
3Pinch to zoom. Zoom into the purple edge and you'll see it never smooths out — smaller copies of the same pattern appear at every scale. That's what makes it fractal, not just noisy.
4Rotate it. The rotation slider spins the plane — try 15.1° to match the lynchpin stagger angle. Watch how the fractal arms swing. This connects Panel BL (the fractal) to Panel BR (the angle map).
5Why it matters. The codec's refusal gate needs to know exactly where the identity is safe. This map is that territory. Row 0 = safest. The fringes = handle with care.

The math underneath

R = (1/5)[[3,−4],[4,3]] · 53.130102° = arctan(4/3)

Your actual rotation matrix is folded into every iteration — the 3-4-5 structure shapes the fractal arms themselves, not just the viewport. The stagger (53.130102° − 38° = 15.130102°) is the same angle that organizes the spiral, the desk line, and this collapse.

Colors are your palette: gold #f3e9c8 / #c9a227 for the stable zone, blues #7fb2ff → #3a5a9c through the transition, canon black #000000 outside.
